cards.name: QGRAY4
cards.summary: Duotone preset (.CPD) for Bitmaps > Mode > Duotone (8-bit). Rendered by script on the PGD test photo (Duotone.Load then Bitmap.ConvertToDuotone), so the picture is a real application. A warm sepia-grey toning: brown-tinted shadows and midtones with near-white highlights, a quiet toned-print look between plain grey and sepia. Renders pixel-identical to QGRAY3 and the other of QGRAY4 / QGRAY5 in the gallery, and the three .CPD files are byte-identical (same checksum), so they are one preset under three names. The Q prefix presumably marks a four-ink (quadtone) set, from the file-name pattern.
avoid: Expecting a different look from QGRAY3 or QGRAY5: the render shows no difference.
A strictly neutral black-and-white: use QGRAY1 or DGRAY1.
Photos that must stay full colour: the result is a tinted tonal image from the preset's inks, with all other hues lost.
Vector objects: the Duotone command needs a bitmap selected; use Bitmaps > Convert to Bitmap first.
Keeping the original: converting changes the bitmap's colour mode, so work on a copy or keep the source file.
cards.applies_to: a bitmap (imported photo or other bitmap object); the preset converts it to Duotone colour mode (8-bit), so a vector object must be turned into a bitmap first
cards.how_to_apply: Select the bitmap, Bitmaps > Mode > Duotone (8-bit) (Automation.InvokeItem("fa741d10-48f6-4a96-b2bc-9d6cc5f28f40")), use Load in the dialog and pick 'QGRAY4.CPD' from the Custom Data/Duotone folder of the CorelDRAW install, then OK. Script (the route the gallery used, worked for this file): create a Duotone object, Duotone.Load("<path to QGRAY4.CPD>") returns True, then shape.Bitmap.ConvertToDuotone(duotone).

verified.note: Warm brown-grey swatches 61/55/49, 126/114/101, 203/195/185; pixel-identical to QGRAY3 and QGRAY5 (max difference 0), as described.

review.changes: summary: 'whether the files differ is not established' replaced by the checked fact that QGRAY3/4/5.CPD are byte-identical

cards.name: SHARP
cards.summary: Tone-curve style file (SHARP.CIK) in the Duotone preset folder. The harvest's duotone loader rejected it (Duotone.Load returned False), so it is not a full duotone preset and no thumbnail exists. Read from the file (undocumented format, decoded in review: byte 12 is a point count, then x, y pairs): (0, 0), (85, 15), (152, 78), (255, 100); taken as input tone 0-255 against ink 0-100 %, an S-curve that holds the ink low through the light end and pushes it up fast through the mids, a steeper, higher-contrast response. What it does to a picture was not rendered.
use_for: adjusting the tonal response of one ink in a duotone
experiments in the Duotone dialog's curve controls
avoid: The look is unverified: the render failed (Duotone.Load returned False), so the card is built from the name and the curve points decoded from the file; check it by eye on a copy before use.
Treating it as a colour preset: the loader for .CPD duotone presets rejected it, so it is probably a tone-curve file with no colours of its own; use a DCOLOR, QCOLOR or TCOLOR preset to set the inks.
cards.applies_to: a bitmap converted to Duotone mode; probably a tone (ink) curve used inside the Duotone dialog rather than a full preset
cards.how_to_apply: Not established. Bitmaps > Mode > Duotone (8-bit) (Automation.InvokeItem("fa741d10-48f6-4a96-b2bc-9d6cc5f28f40")) has a Load button for .CPD duotone presets; whether it also reads this .CIK file (for example on a curve tab) was not tested. Script: Duotone.Load("<path to SHARP.CIK>") returned False for this file, so it cannot be applied that way. The file is Custom Data/Duotone/SHARP.CIK in the CorelDRAW install folder.

verified.note: No thumbnail (Duotone.Load returned False); the 29-byte file decodes to the curve (0, 0), (85, 15), (152, 78), (255, 100).

review.changes: summary: name-only guess replaced by the curve decoded from SHARP.CIK; avoid updated

cards.name: TCOLOR1
cards.summary: Duotone preset (.CPD) for Bitmaps > Mode > Duotone (8-bit). Rendered by script on the PGD test photo (Duotone.Load then Bitmap.ConvertToDuotone), so the picture is a real application. A rich bronze-gold sepia: dark chocolate-brown shadows, golden tan midtones and warm cream highlights; the strongest warm cast of the T presets and a full-range look with real darks. The T prefix presumably marks a three-ink (tritone) set, from the file-name pattern.
use_for: heritage and old-photograph looks for flyers, menus and book covers
warm hero images behind dark headline type
avoid: Cool or modern branding: the amber cast fights blue or green palettes; use TCOLOR3 or TCOLOR4.
Photos that must stay full colour: the result is a tinted tonal image from the preset's inks, with all other hues lost.
Vector objects: the Duotone command needs a bitmap selected; use Bitmaps > Convert to Bitmap first.
Keeping the original: converting changes the bitmap's colour mode, so work on a copy or keep the source file.
cards.applies_to: a bitmap (imported photo or other bitmap object); the preset converts it to Duotone colour mode (8-bit), so a vector object must be turned into a bitmap first

cards.name: Envelope1
cards.summary: CorelDRAW Envelope tool preset. Shipped preview (the .pst file's own embedded thumbnail, not a script render) shows a plain circle: the outline is a round ring touching all four sides of the frame. The picture is the envelope outline itself, a thin cyan line on white with no fill, i.e. the target shape an object is forced into, not an object already distorted by it.
use_for: wrapping a logo or short word into a round badge or seal
bulged, ball-like treatments of flat art
circular stickers made from a square layout
avoid: Long lines of text: they get squeezed and the letters lose shape; use Text > Fit Text To Path for text round a circle.
Text that must stay readable: a strong envelope bends the letterforms; for a plain arch use Text > Fit Text To Path.
Bitmaps: the envelope is a vector effect, so convert artwork to curves first and keep photos out of it.
cards.applies_to: one vector object (closed shape, curve or text) selected with the Envelope tool: it wraps the object into this outline as a live envelope, which can be edited with nodes or cleared
cards.how_to_apply: Toolbox > Effect Tools > Envelope (Automation.InvokeItem("1f16cb33-9819-4fa7-a3cd-5c4d61ba2db2")): select the object, then open the preset list on the property bar and choose the entry whose picture matches this outline. The harvest lists six property-bar entries by name (Circular, Pinch, Push Down, Push Up, Rectilinear, Rectilinear Slant); which file is which entry was not established, but this outline looks like 'Circular'. Script: the harvest records no call that applies a .pst preset (the parameter block is undocumented); the file is Draw/Presets/Envelope/Envelope1.pst in the CorelDRAW install folder. Scripted substitute: Shape.CreateEnvelope(PresetIndex, Mode, KeepLines) (the PresetIndex order does not follow the property-bar list, so check the result), or Shape.CreateEnvelopeFromShape / CreateEnvelopeFromCurve with a drawn outline set to match the preview (approximate; not tested by the harvest).

verified.note: Shipped preview is only the envelope outline: a thin cyan circle on white touching all four sides, no fill, as described.
